vocab.context: The single most important particle. 'Ore wa Uzumaki Naruto da!' — marks what the sentence is about. Every anime intro uses it.
Marks who actually performs the action. 'Ichigo ga tatakau' — Ichigo is the one fighting. Often contrasted with は for nuance.
Marks what gets acted on. 'Getsuga wo hanate!' — release the Getsuga! Hear it before every anime special attack.
The Swiss army particle. Direction, time, indirect object. 'Tokyo ni iku' (go to Tokyo), 'Ore ni makasero' (leave it to me).
Where something happens or what you use to do it. 'Kenshin ga katana de kiru' — Kenshin cuts with a katana. 'Maito Gai ga dojo de renshuu suru' — Guy trains at the dojo.
Possession or noun modification. 'Sharingan no chikara' — the power of the Sharingan. 'Ore no nakama' — my crewmates.
Connects nouns exhaustively or marks quoted speech. 'Luffy to Zoro' — Luffy and Zoro. Also marks what someone said or thought.
'Ore mo iku!' — I'm going too! What Chopper shouts when Luffy runs into danger. The particle that refuses to let a friend go alone.
The soft contradiction particle. 'Suki dakedo, ienai' — I like you, but I can't say it. Romance arcs run on this word. Also softens requests: 'Ii kedo...' — it's fine, but...
Lists items without exhausting them. In Demon Slayer, gear lists use ya — sword, whetstone, and more. Softer than と — implies the list continues beyond what's named.
Softer, more poetic direction than に. 'Sunny-gou wa shin sekai he' — the Sunny sails toward the New World. The particle of longing and journey — used in endings, not battles.

Origin or reason. 'Naze tatakau? Nakama ga iru kara!' — Why fight? Because my nakama are here! Direct and passionate. More casual than ので — use kara for gut-level conviction, node for polite explanation.

meanings.en: until / up to / as far as

vocab.context: Sets a limit in time or space. 'Saigo made akiramenai' — I won't give up until the very end. Classic anime final-battle phrase.
Comparison particle. 'Dare yori mo tsuyoi' — stronger than anyone alive. Vegeta says it about himself. Gojo says it calmly. How you know a character thinks they've already won.
Turns any statement into a question just by adding it at the end. 'Omae wa nakama ka?' — Are you friend or enemy? The pause before this word lands is its own dramatic device.
Seeks agreement or softens a statement. 'Sugoi, ne?' — Amazing, right? Common in slice-of-life and romance anime to build connection.
Announces something the listener doesn't know yet. 'Ore wa kita yo!' — I'm here! Assertive and confident — heroes use this constantly.
The shonen hero particle. 'Iku zo!' — here we go! Naruto, Goku, Ichigo — every protagonist has a signature phrase ending in ぞ. More forceful than よ, less rough than ぜ.
Two meanings in one syllable. Falling intonation = prohibition: 'Sore wa suru na!' — Don't do that! (Kakashi stopping Naruto). Rising = soft agreement: 'Ii na' — nice, right?
Rougher than よ, more street-level than ぞ. 'Ore ga katsu ze!' — I'm gonna win! Rivals, delinquents, and loud side characters favor this. Heroes level up to ぞ when they get serious.

meanings.pt-BR: porque / por isso (motivo educado e suave)
meanings.es: porque / así que (razón educada y suave)

vocab.context: Politer and softer than から when giving reasons. 'Tsuyoku naritai node, renshuu shimasu' — I want to get stronger, so I train. The reason a disciplined character gives before acting. (See から for the passionate version.)
Attaches to the past-tense form to mean 'if/when this happens'. 'Moshi shindara — tatakau' — If I die, fight on. The particle of ultimatums, desperate gambles, and conditional vows.
